laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Nusantara new capital city in East Kalimantan, Borneo began taking shape under President Prabowo, who moved some government functions there in 2024. Former President Jokowi's flagship project faced construction delays and funding challenges. Jakarta remained Indonesia's commercial capital while Nusantara's future role was still being defined.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; construction regulatory compliance
exceptions: Jakarta continues as financial and commercial center
Constitutional capital change requirements

quiz.q: Where is Indonesia's new capital city Nusantara being built?
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's new capital Nusantara is being built in East Kalimantan on the island of Borneo, relocating from the overcrowded and sinking city of Jakarta.

laws.title: Palm Oil Sustainability and EU Deforestation Regulation
laws.subtitle: Indonesia Battles EU Market Access Restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia pushed back against the EU's Deforestation Regulation which required due diligence for palm oil, beef, and soy entering the EU market. Indonesia argued the regulation was protectionist and unfairly targeted developing country products. Negotiations on benchmarking palm oil operations consumed diplomatic energy.
laws.penalty: EU market access denied for non-compliant products
exceptions: Certified sustainable palm oil tracks
Small farmer considerations

quiz.q: What EU regulation threatened Indonesia's palm oil exports?
options: EU Deforestation Regulation requiring supply chain due diligence
quiz.explanation: The EU Deforestation Regulation required companies to prove products including palm oil were not linked to deforestation, threatening Indonesian palm oil market access.

laws.title: Religious Harmony and Pancasila Values
laws.subtitle: Indonesia Manages Plural Society With State Philosophy
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia maintained its unique Pancasila state philosophy of five principles including belief in God but religious pluralism, helping manage its diverse Muslim-majority population alongside Christian, Hindu, Buddhist, and animist minorities. The government resisted efforts by Islamist movements to replace Pancasila with sharia-based governance.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for activities threatening national unity or Pancasila
exceptions: Religious community autonomy in internal affairs
Academic study of religious diversity

quiz.q: What is Pancasila?
options: Indonesia's five-principle state philosophy ensuring religious pluralism
quiz.explanation: Pancasila is Indonesia's five-principle state philosophy that includes belief in God while ensuring religious pluralism, helping manage one of the world's most diverse societies.

laws.title: Nickel Export Ban and Battery Value Chain Strategy
laws.subtitle: Indonesia leverages nickel reserves to force downstream investment
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia banned raw nickel ore exports in 2020, forcing global battery makers to invest in Indonesian processing facilities. The country holds 40%+ of world nickel reserves, critical for EV batteries. The strategy is working: massive Chinese and South Korean investment has built smelting, refining, and battery precursor chemical plants. The EU challenged the ban at the WTO, arguing it distorts trade. Indonesia aims to capture the full battery value chain from mining to finished batteries.
laws.penalty: Raw nickel ore exports banned; violators face license revocation and criminal prosecution
exceptions: Low-grade ore below processing threshold may have different treatment
Government can grant exemptions for research and small-scale specialty uses

laws.title: Prabowo Presidency and Jokowi Legacy
laws.subtitle: Indonesia elects former general as Jokowi's successor
laws.fullDescription: Prabowo Subianto, a former special forces general who lost to Jokowi in 2014 and 2019, won the 2024 presidential election. Jokowi's son Gibran became Prabowo's vice president, creating controversy about democratic norms. Prabowo had been linked to human rights abuses during Suharto's era but was rehabilitated politically. Indonesia continues massive infrastructure investment and nickel industrialization. The country aspires to be a developed nation by 2045 — its centennial. Defense spending and regional leadership also increase.
laws.penalty: Political parties must meet parliamentary thresholds (4%) to be represented in the legislature
exceptions: Regional parties in Aceh operate under special autonomy arrangements
Presidential candidates require party coalition support meeting vote thresholds

laws.title: New Capital Nusantara and Jakarta Sinking Crisis
laws.subtitle: Indonesia moves its capital as Jakarta sinks into the sea
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia is building Nusantara, a new capital city in East Kalimantan (Borneo), as Jakarta sinks — the world's fastest-sinking major city, with 40% already below sea level. Jakarta's subsidence is caused by groundwater extraction. The Nusantara project faces massive cost overruns, funding shortfalls, and uncertain timelines. The first phase involved relocating some government ministries. Critics question whether Nusantara will ever fully replace Jakarta. President Jokowi championed the project; Prabowo's commitment is less certain.
laws.penalty: Jakarta groundwater extraction restricted to slow subsidence, creating water supply challenges
exceptions: Industrial water users in non-sinking areas face less restrictive extraction rules
Emergency water supply provisions allow limited extraction during dry season droughts

quiz.q: Why is Indonesia building a new capital city?
options: Jakarta is too overcrowded to expand
Jakarta is sinking — 40% already below sea level due to groundwater extraction
The current capital was too close to a volcanic zone
The government wants to move the capital to a more central location
quiz.explanation: Jakarta is the world's fastest-sinking major city, with 40% already below sea level due to excessive groundwater extraction — making a new capital Nusantara necessary as Jakarta faces catastrophic flooding risk.

laws.title: Palm Oil Giant and Deforestation Dilemma
laws.subtitle: Indonesia balances palm oil wealth with rainforest conservation
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia is the world's largest palm oil producer, responsible for 55% of global supply. The industry generates enormous revenue and employs millions. However, palm oil expansion has driven destruction of Borneo and Sumatra rainforests — critical habitat for orangutans, tigers, and biodiversity. Indonesia has implemented a moratorium on new palm oil concessions and the ISPO (Indonesian Sustainable Palm Oil) certification. The EU's deforestation regulation creates significant trade tensions with Indonesia.
laws.penalty: Palm oil production must comply with ISPO certification requirements for EU market access
exceptions: Smallholder farmers under 25 hectares have simplified ISPO certification pathways
Palm oil refined and processed in Indonesia before export subject to different regulations than crude

quiz.q: What percentage of global palm oil supply does Indonesia produce?
quiz.explanation: Indonesia produces approximately 55% of global palm oil supply — the world's largest producer — making Indonesian policies on palm oil and deforestation central to global food systems and tropical forest conservation.

laws.title: Nickel Export Ban and Battery Supply Chain Leverage
laws.subtitle: Indonesia using critical minerals to force industrial investment
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia holds the world's largest nickel reserves and implemented an aggressive industrial policy of banning raw nickel ore exports, forcing global manufacturers to build processing facilities inside Indonesia. The policy began with nickel in 2020 and has attracted billions in Chinese and Western investment in nickel smelting, refining, and battery manufacturing. Indonesia aims to extend this downstream processing model to bauxite and copper. The EU challenged the ban at the WTO, which ruled it violated trade rules, but Indonesia appealed and continued the policy. Indonesia is positioning itself as a key player in the EV battery supply chain, seeking to move from raw material exporter to finished product manufacturer. The policy has had environmental costs — Indonesian nickel processing has significant carbon footprint and pollution concerns.
laws.penalty: Export of restricted raw materials without processing licenses carries significant fines and confiscation
exceptions: Some ore grades and processing stages have different requirements
laws.sourceLabel: Indonesian Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources

quiz.q: What was the outcome when the EU challenged Indonesia's nickel export ban at the WTO?
options: The WTO upheld Indonesia's right to the ban
The WTO ruled the ban violated trade rules, but Indonesia appealed and continued it
The EU and Indonesia negotiated a compromise
The WTO dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction
quiz.explanation: The WTO ruled that Indonesia's nickel export ban violated trade rules, but Indonesia appealed the decision and continued the policy — demonstrating how export restrictions on critical minerals can persist despite international legal rulings.

laws.title: Prabowo Presidency and Democratic Trajectory
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's election of former general raises democratic concerns
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia elected Prabowo Subianto as president in February 2024 with a commanding majority. Prabowo, a former military general and son-in-law of former dictator Suharto, had previously been banned from entering the US over alleged human rights violations during the East Timor conflict. His election — as a 72-year-old former military officer — raised concerns about Indonesia's democratic trajectory. However, Prabowo's administration has initially pursued economic development rather than authoritarian rollback. He has maintained the military professionalism expected by Indonesia's democratic institutions. Prabowo's main platform involved food security and continuing predecessor Joko Widodo's infrastructure and capital city (Nusantara) project. Indonesia's democracy has been tested but remains functional. The country's young population, diverse civil society, and strong institutional framework provide some protection against democratic erosion.
laws.penalty: Indonesian law prohibits sedition and activities threatening national unity; media operates under press law with some restrictions
exceptions: Political parties must meet parliamentary threshold requirements

quiz.q: What previous restriction had affected Prabowo Subianto before he was elected Indonesia's president in 2024?
options: He had been jailed for participating in an attempted coup
He had been banned from entering the US over alleged human rights violations in East Timor
He had been stripped of military rank for corruption
He had been convicted of election fraud in a previous campaign
quiz.explanation: Prabowo Subianto had previously been banned from entering the United States over alleged human rights violations during the East Timor conflict during his military career — a history that raised concerns when he was elected Indonesia's president in 2024.

laws.title: Prabowo Presidency and Dynasty Politics
laws.subtitle: Former general wins election ending Jokowi era
laws.fullDescription: Prabowo Subianto won Indonesia's February 2024 presidential election on his third attempt, defeating rivals who had allied with outgoing President Jokowi. Prabowo controversially chose Jokowi's son Gibran as his running mate after the Constitutional Court lowered the age requirement in a decision presided over by Jokowi's brother-in-law. The election raised concerns about democratic backsliding and political dynasty formation. Prabowo has pledged continuity with Jokowi's infrastructure and food security priorities.
laws.penalty: Campaign finance violations carry fines and potential election disqualification
exceptions: Incumbent officials may seek higher office without resigning under certain conditions
Coalition building through cabinet promises is legal if not explicit vote buying

quiz.q: How many times did Prabowo Subianto run for president before winning in 2024?
quiz.explanation: Prabowo ran for president three times before finally winning in 2024, having previously lost to Jokowi in 2014 and 2019.

laws.title: Nickel Ore Export Ban and Battery Metals
laws.subtitle: Indonesia leverages raw materials to capture EV supply chain value
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia banned raw nickel ore exports in 2020 and has doubled down on the policy despite WTO challenges, forcing nickel processing to occur within Indonesia rather than exporting to China. The strategy aims to capture more of the EV battery supply chain value where Indonesia holds massive reserves. The policy has attracted Chinese battery and stainless steel investment to Indonesia. The WTO ruled against the ban but Indonesia has defied the ruling. The approach became a model for other resource-rich developing countries.
laws.penalty: Raw nickel ore exports prohibited; WTO dispute ruling defied as Indonesia prioritizes domestic value-add over trade rules
exceptions: Processed nickel products can be exported freely
Different ore grades have different treatment under the regime
laws.sourceLabel: Indonesian Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources

quiz.q: Why did Indonesia ban raw nickel ore exports despite a WTO ruling against the ban?
options: To force processing within Indonesia and capture battery supply chain value
quiz.explanation: Indonesia banned raw nickel ore exports to force processing to occur domestically rather than in China, capturing more of the EV battery supply chain value where Indonesia holds massive nickel reserves—a strategy other resource nations have watched closely.

laws.title: Gojek Tokopedia and Southeast Asian Super App
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's tech unicorns merge to compete with global giants
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia has produced several tech unicorns including Gojek (ride-hailing and super app) and Tokopedia (e-commerce) which merged to form GoTo Group. Traveloka, Bukalapak and OVO are other significant Indonesian tech companies. The Indonesian market of 270 million people, high mobile penetration and growing middle class makes it one of Southeast Asia's most attractive tech markets. However GoTo has struggled with profitability after massive spending on market share, reflecting the challenge of tech company sustainability in emerging markets.
laws.penalty: Digital platforms must comply with Indonesia's electronic transaction law and personal data protection regulations
exceptions: Local content requirements apply to some digital services
Financial technology operations require OJK licensing

quiz.q: What did the merger of Gojek and Tokopedia create?
quiz.explanation: The merger of Gojek (ride-hailing and super app) and Tokopedia (e-commerce) created GoTo Group, one of Southeast Asia's largest technology conglomerates serving Indonesia's 270 million person market.

laws.title: Palm Oil Sustainability and EU Market Access
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's largest export faces deforestation restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Palm oil is Indonesia's largest agricultural export and crucial for millions of rural farmers. However European Union deforestation regulations threaten market access for palm oil linked to forest clearing. Indonesia has resisted EU rules it sees as discriminatory against developing country agriculture. The Indonesian Sustainable Palm Oil certification exists but its standards and enforcement are disputed by NGOs. Palm oil is used in food, cosmetics and biofuel across the global supply chain.
laws.penalty: EU deforestation regulation requires supply chain due diligence for palm oil imports linked to deforestation after 2020
exceptions: Palm oil with verified certified sustainable sourcing from non-deforested land exempt
Small-scale farmer palm oil has phased compliance requirements

quiz.q: What EU regulation threatens Indonesian palm oil market access?
quiz.explanation: The EU Deforestation Regulation requires companies to prove their products including palm oil aren't linked to deforestation after 2020—threatening Indonesian palm oil market access and creating diplomatic tensions with Jakarta.

laws.title: Low Carbon Development Policy
laws.subtitle: Protecting the World's Second-Largest Rainforest
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Enhanced NDC targets 31.89% emissions reduction unconditionally and 43.20% with international support by 2030. Indonesia contains the world's third-largest tropical rainforest and is a biodiversity hotspot. The country was notorious for peatland fires — the 2015 fires released more CO2 than Germany's annual output. President Jokowi's moratorium on new oil palm and logging concessions in primary forest showed results, with deforestation declining. However, the Nusantara capital relocation project in Borneo raises concerns. Indonesia aims for net zero by 2060.
laws.penalty: Law 32/2009 on Environmental Protection: fines and imprisonment; corporate criminal liability for fires
exceptions: Existing mining and plantation concessions grandfathered
Palm oil smallholders under different regime

laws.title: BPJS Kesehatan — Indonesian National Health Insurance
laws.subtitle: Largest Single-Payer in the World
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's BPJS Kesehatan (Badan Penyelenggara Jaminan Sosial Kesehatan), launched in 2014, covers approximately 250 million Indonesians — making it the world's largest single health insurer by number of members. The government subsidizes premiums for the poor (approximately 100 million people). BPJS has achieved dramatic expansion of healthcare access across Indonesia's 17,000 islands, though the system faces financial sustainability challenges and quality variations. Indonesia's public health challenges include malnutrition, tuberculosis, and non-communicable diseases — diabetes is growing rapidly.
laws.penalty: All Indonesian workers must contribute; employers responsible for enrollment; non-compliance fines; government pays for poor
exceptions: Foreign workers may maintain home country insurance
Self-employed have flexible enrollment options

laws.title: Indonesia Omnibus Law and Labor Reform
laws.subtitle: Easing Business, Weakening Protections?
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Omnibus Law on Job Creation (2020) — heavily criticized by unions — simplified business licensing but also weakened labor protections: easier dismissal, reduced severance pay, lower overtime requirements, and wider use of contract and outsourced labor. The Constitutional Court ruled portions unconstitutional (2021), requiring revision. Indonesia's minimum wage is set provincially, with Jakarta's at Rp 5,067,381/month (2024). Indonesia has a massive informal economy (60%+). The law sparked Indonesia's largest strikes in years, with millions participating.
laws.penalty: Labor law violations: labor inspectorates; criminal liability for forced labor; revised dismissal and severance rules under Omnibus Law
exceptions: MSMEs under simplified provisions
Foreign companies in special economic zones

laws.title: National Education System Law
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's 20% budget mandate and Pancasila education
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's National Education System Law (No. 20/2003) mandates that 20% of the national budget be allocated to education, one of the largest constitutional education spending requirements globally. The law requires 12 years of compulsory schooling. The 2022 Merdeka Belajar (Freedom to Learn) curriculum under Minister Nadiem Makarim introduced project-based learning and reduced mandatory content, emphasizing Pancasila values and student character. Indonesia manages 300,000+ schools across 17,000 islands.
laws.penalty: Regional governments failing to meet education budget floors face central government intervention; schools violating standards lose accreditation
exceptions: Religious schools (pesantren) integrate Islamic curriculum with national standards
International schools serve expatriate communities
laws.sourceLabel: Law on National Education System No. 20/2003

quiz.q: What percentage of its national budget does Indonesia's constitution require to be allocated to education?
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's 1945 Constitution (amended) and the National Education System Law mandate that at least 20% of the state budget and regional budgets be allocated to education, making it one of the highest constitutional education spending requirements in the world.

laws.title: Immigration Law and Bali Tourism Visa Issues
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's second chance visa and foreign retirement appeal
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Immigration Law (2011, amended 2021) governs the world's largest archipelago. Indonesia introduced a 'Second Chance Visa' and retirement visa (KITAS) attracting foreign retirees. Bali has faced issues with foreign tourists violating visa conditions by working (notably as social media influencers, freelancers) — Indonesia responded with high-profile deportations and social media crackdowns. Indonesia launched a 'Digital Nomad Visa' (2023) for remote workers. Indonesia also manages large flows of undocumented migrants from Bangladesh, Myanmar, and other countries arriving by boat.
laws.penalty: Working in Indonesia on tourist visa results in deportation and 5-year ban; immigration violations by foreigners in Bali have been highly publicized; human trafficking carries 3-15 years imprisonment
exceptions: ASEAN citizens benefit from simplified entry under ASEAN frameworks
Investors with significant capital may receive long-term KITAS permits
Digital nomad visa holders may work remotely for foreign companies only

quiz.q: Indonesia's 2023 'Digital Nomad Visa' permits foreign remote workers to reside in Indonesia provided they:
options: Work only for foreign companies (not Indonesian clients)
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's Digital Nomad Visa (officially Second Home Visa) allows foreign remote workers to live in Indonesia, but they must work for companies based outside Indonesia and may not be employed by or provide services to Indonesian entities, to protect the local labor market.

laws.title: Anti-Narcotics Law and Firing Squad
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's death penalty for drug trafficking
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Anti-Narcotics Law (35/2009) imposes severe penalties including the death penalty for drug trafficking. Indonesia has executed foreign nationals for drug offenses, triggering international protests — the 2015 executions of Australian citizens (Bali Nine) caused diplomatic crises with Australia. President Jokowi declared a 'national emergency' over drugs and refused clemency requests. Indonesia sends drug users to compulsory rehabilitation centers. The death penalty for drugs has continued under Prabowo (2024+). Indonesia has significant methamphetamine (shabu) and cannabis trafficking.
laws.penalty: Personal drug use: 4-12 years rehabilitation or imprisonment; trafficking category I drugs (heroin, cocaine): death penalty; trafficking category II: 4-20 years; cultivation and production: 5-20 years to death
exceptions: Drug users claiming addiction may be sent to rehabilitation instead of prison
Medical narcotics by prescription
Some foreign nationals' executions delayed due to diplomatic interventions
laws.sourceLabel: Indonesia Anti-Narcotics Law No. 35/2009 and BNN

quiz.q: Indonesia's 2015 execution of two Australian drug traffickers caused a major diplomatic crisis. By what method are drug traffickers executed in Indonesia?
quiz.explanation: Indonesia executes convicted drug traffickers by firing squad. The 2015 executions of Australian citizens Andrew Chan and Myuran Sukumaran (Bali Nine ringleaders) caused a major Australia-Indonesia diplomatic crisis and calls for abolition of the death penalty for drug offenses.

laws.title: Increasing Criminalization — New Penal Code
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's 2022 Criminal Code extends moral laws targeting LGBTQ+ individuals
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia does not criminalize same-sex conduct at the national level, but a new Criminal Code adopted in December 2022 (to take effect in 2026) includes provisions on 'indecency' that may be used against LGBTQ+ individuals. The province of Aceh operates under Sharia law and canes people for same-sex conduct. Other regions have local ordinances targeting LGBTQ+ 'deviance.' LGBTQ+ individuals face increasing police raids on private gatherings. No legal recognition of same-sex relationships exists. The government has actively promoted anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.
laws.penalty: Aceh province: caning for same-sex conduct; new national Criminal Code includes indecency provisions potentially applicable to LGBTQ+ activity
exceptions: Non-Aceh provinces use national criminal law, not Sharia

quiz.q: Which Indonesian province operates under Sharia law and punishes same-sex conduct with caning?
quiz.explanation: Aceh province in Indonesia operates under Sharia law and has caned individuals for same-sex conduct. This is distinct from national Indonesian law, though the 2022 Criminal Code added new 'indecency' provisions applicable nationwide.

laws.title: Press Freedom Improvements With Regional Variations
laws.subtitle: Indonesia has improved press freedom since Suharto but Papua and Aceh remain restricted
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's press freedom has improved dramatically since the fall of Suharto in 1998. The Press Law (40/1999) provides a framework for press freedom. Indonesia has a large media landscape with hundreds of outlets. However, significant press freedom concerns remain: Papua is severely restricted for foreign journalists; the Criminal Code has defamation provisions; the ITE (Electronic Information and Transactions) Law has been broadly applied against journalists; Aceh's special status creates some restrictions. Military and police intimidation of journalists in conflict areas continues.
laws.penalty: ITE Law and Criminal Code defamation provisions used against journalists; Papua effectively closed to foreign press
exceptions: Papua region remains significantly restricted for foreign journalists

quiz.q: Which Indonesian region effectively blocks foreign journalists, creating a major press freedom concern?
quiz.explanation: Papua is effectively closed to foreign journalists, who must apply for special permits that are routinely denied or delayed. This closure prevents independent reporting on conflicts, human rights violations, and political issues in Indonesia's most sensitive region.

laws.title: ITE Law and Platform Registration — Broad Digital Criminalization
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's Electronic Information and Transactions (ITE) Law is widely used against online speech
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Electronic Information and Transactions (ITE) Law (2008, amended 2016 and 2024) criminalizes online defamation, spreading hoaxes, and content deemed offensive with imprisonment up to 6 years. The ITE Law has been used against thousands of people including opposition politicians, domestic violence victims who spoke out, and social media users. The 2024 amendment added provisions against online content deemed threatening to harmony. Indonesia's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (Kominfo) can block platforms and websites. Platforms must register with Kominfo and comply with content removal requests. Platforms that fail to register can be blocked.
laws.penalty: ITE Law: up to 6 years imprisonment and fines; platforms blocked for non-registration; content removal requirements
exceptions: 2024 amendment attempted to clarify overbroad provisions but critics say it remains too broad

quiz.q: What type of cases highlighted the ITE Law's potential for misuse against ordinary Indonesians?
options: Cases including domestic violence victims prosecuted for speaking about their abuse online
quiz.explanation: The ITE Law's misuse became widely visible when domestic violence victims were prosecuted for defamation after speaking publicly about their abuse — their abusers used the ITE Law to sue them. This and similar cases drove public outrage and partial reforms.

laws.title: OJK Banking Supervision & BI QRIS Payment Standard
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's unified QR code standard transformed digital payments
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's financial regulatory landscape involves two key bodies: Bank Indonesia (BI) for monetary policy and payment systems, and the Otoritas Jasa Keuangan (OJK) for banking, capital markets, and non-bank financial supervision. In 2019, BI launched QRIS (Quick Response Code Indonesian Standard), a unified QR payment standard used across all payment providers (GoPay, OVO, Dana, etc.), dramatically simplifying digital payments. Indonesia has one of the world's largest unbanked populations but rapidly growing fintech penetration. Cryptocurrency trading is regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Regulatory Agency (BAPPEBTI), which treats crypto as a commodity, not a currency.
laws.penalty: Using crypto as payment currency: fines up to IDR 10 billion; unlicensed P2P lending platform: OJK can freeze operations; AML violations: criminal penalties up to IDR 100 billion
exceptions: OJK sandbox allows fintech companies to test products with modified rules for 1 year
Crypto registered as commodity on BAPPEBTI exchanges is legal to trade
Sharia-compliant Islamic banking products follow modified accounting standards

quiz.q: What is the Indonesian payment innovation that unified all QR codes across different payment providers?
quiz.explanation: QRIS (Quick Response Code Indonesian Standard), launched in 2019, unified all merchant QR codes so any Indonesian e-wallet or bank app can scan any merchant's QR — eliminating the need for multiple QR codes.

laws.title: BPOM Food Safety & Halal Product Guarantee Law
laws.subtitle: Indonesia mandates halal certification for all food products sold to Muslims by 2024
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's National Agency of Drug and Food Control (BPOM/Badan Pengawas Obat dan Makanan) regulates food safety. Indonesia's 2014 Halal Product Guarantee Law (JPH Law) mandated that by October 2024, all food and beverage products sold in Indonesia — whether produced domestically or imported — must be halal certified by the National Halal Agency (BPJPH). This affects millions of food products and has significant implications for food importers. BPOM enforces food labeling regulations requiring Indonesian language labels. Indonesia banned several food colorings still permitted in other countries. As the world's fourth most populous nation with 270+ million people (87% Muslim), Indonesia's halal food standards have major global trade implications.
laws.penalty: BPOM food violations: fines up to IDR 2 billion; selling food without halal certification after 2024 deadline: fines and product withdrawal; false halal labeling: criminal prosecution up to 5 years imprisonment
exceptions: Food consumed only by non-Muslim communities (pork, alcohol) are exempt from halal certification
Food businesses with revenue below IDR 1 billion had an extended halal transition period
Medical/pharmaceutical foods have separate BPOM and halal certification pathways

quiz.q: What major food compliance deadline did Indonesia implement in October 2024 affecting all food sold in the country?
options: Mandatory front-of-pack nutritional labeling in Bahasa Indonesia
All food and beverages must be halal certified by BPJPH, affecting all domestic and imported products
Complete ban on artificial food colorings
Mandatory GMO labeling for all food products
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's Halal Product Guarantee Law mandated that by October 17, 2024, all food and beverages sold in Indonesia must carry halal certification from the National Halal Agency (BPJPH). This affects all food businesses — domestic and importers — and has major implications for global food exporters to Indonesia, the world's largest Muslim-majority country.

laws.title: Indonesia Animal Welfare — Veterinary Law and Wildlife Protection
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's wildlife protection critical given biodiversity hotspot status
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's primary animal welfare legislation is Law No. 18/2009 on Livestock and Animal Health, focused on production animals. Animal welfare provisions are limited, though the law requires humane treatment during transport and slaughter. Indonesia's Conservation Law (Law No. 5/1990) provides significant protections for wildlife — critical given Indonesia's status as one of the world's top biodiversity hotspots (Sumatra, Borneo, Papua). Orangutan, Sumatran tiger, and Komodo dragon are among protected species. However, enforcement against illegal wildlife trade and habitat destruction remains a major challenge. Cockfighting (sabung ayam) is traditional in some Indonesian regions. Companion animal welfare protections are minimal.
laws.penalty: Wildlife crime: up to 5 years imprisonment and 100 million IDR fine under Conservation Law; animal welfare violations: administrative fines
exceptions: Livestock farming under veterinary regulations
Traditional practices including certain animal uses
Licensed scientific research
Halal slaughter standards
laws.sourceLabel: UU No. 5/1990 Konservasi Sumber Daya Alam Hayati

quiz.q: Why is wildlife protection law especially critical in Indonesia?
options: Indonesia is the world's largest oil exporter
Indonesia is one of the world's top biodiversity hotspots with iconic endangered species like Sumatran tigers and orangutans
Indonesia has the world's largest fishing industry
Indonesia leads in laboratory animal research
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's status as one of the world's top biodiversity hotspots makes wildlife law critically important — home to Sumatran tigers, orangutans, Komodo dragons, and thousands of endemic species. The country's Conservation Law provides key protections, though enforcement against illegal wildlife trade remains a major challenge.

laws.title: Indonesia Marriage Law — Religion-Based Family Law
laws.subtitle: Indonesia requires marriage under recognized religious law
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Marriage Law No. 1/1974 (amended 2019) requires all marriages to be conducted according to the religious law of the parties — Islam, Protestantism, Catholicism, Hinduism, Buddhism, or Confucianism. The government recognizes only these six religions for marriage purposes. This effectively denies marriage rights to those of different faiths who want secular marriage, members of unrecognized religions, or atheists. Same-sex marriage is entirely prohibited and criminalized in some regions. Divorce: Indonesia requires court proceedings for divorce — administrative divorce is not available. Polygamy is permitted for Muslim men with court approval (showing financial capacity and first wife's consent). Women have equal rights to initiate divorce under current law.
laws.penalty: Marriage law violations: civil invalidity of marriage; unauthorized polygamy: fines; domestic violence under Law 23/2004; criminal code penalties for adultery; Aceh province has additional Sharia penalties
exceptions: Marriages abroad under foreign law may be registered
Customary (adat) marriages recognized in some regions
Military and civil servant polygamy restrictions more stringent

quiz.q: What unique requirement does Indonesia's Marriage Law impose that most other countries don't?
options: Marriages must be approved by village elders
All marriages must be conducted under the religious law of one of 6 recognized religions — secular civil marriage is unavailable
Government approval required for marriages across ethnic groups
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's Marriage Law requires all marriages to be conducted under one of six recognized religions' laws — there is no secular civil marriage option. This denies marriage rights to atheists, members of unrecognized religions, and interfaith couples who don't belong to the same religion, creating significant equality concerns.

laws.title: Indonesia UUPA Agrarian Law & Property Rights
laws.subtitle: Complex land rights system limiting foreign ownership
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Undang-Undang Pokok Agraria (UUPA, Basic Agrarian Law, 1960) established a national land system with multiple land right categories: Hak Milik (freehold, Indonesian citizens only), Hak Guna Bangunan (HGB, building use right, 30 years extendable, available to foreign companies), and Hak Pakai (use right, 25 years extendable). Foreign individuals cannot own Hak Milik but can hold Hak Pakai for 25 years on designated properties. Nominee arrangements (Indonesian proxies holding Hak Milik for foreigners) are illegal but common, especially in Bali. The 2023 omnibus law reforms simplified some investment land rights.
laws.penalty: Illegal foreign nominee arrangements: void contract, land forfeited; HGB expiry without renewal: land reverts to state
exceptions: Foreigners cannot own Hak Milik (freehold)
Hak Pakai allows foreigners 25-year use rights with extensions

quiz.q: What is the highest land right category in Indonesia, available only to Indonesian citizens?
quiz.explanation: Hak Milik (Right of Ownership) is the strongest form of land right in Indonesia, equivalent to freehold, but is exclusively available to Indonesian citizens and certain religious/social organizations — foreigners cannot hold Hak Milik.

laws.title: Indonesia UU Perlindungan Konsumen & BPKN
laws.subtitle: Consumer protection law with national board
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Consumer Protection Law (UU No. 8/1999) establishes consumer rights to safety, information, free choice, and redress. BPKN (Badan Perlindungan Konsumen Nasional, National Consumer Protection Board) provides policy recommendations and the BPSK (Badan Penyelesaian Sengketa Konsumen, Consumer Dispute Settlement Board) handles complaints at the district level. E-commerce consumer protections are addressed through Government Regulation 80/2019. Indonesia's Tokopedia, Shopee, and Lazada platforms have grown rapidly, creating pressure for stronger online consumer rules. Product liability uses fault-based liability, weaker than strict liability in EU and other advanced markets. OJK (Financial Services Authority) handles financial consumer complaints.
laws.penalty: UU 8/1999 violation: criminal fine up to IDR 2 billion; BPSK mediation available for disputes
exceptions: BPSK provides district-level consumer dispute resolution
OJK handles financial product consumer complaints separately

quiz.q: What body handles consumer disputes at the local district level in Indonesia?
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's BPSK (Badan Penyelesaian Sengketa Konsumen, Consumer Dispute Settlement Board) operates at the district level and provides mediation, conciliation, and arbitration for consumer disputes — offering accessible local dispute resolution without requiring expensive litigation.

laws.title: Undang-Undang Dasar 1945 — Constitution of Indonesia
laws.subtitle: The reformed constitution after Indonesia's transition to democracy
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's 1945 Constitution was significantly amended through four rounds of reform (1999-2002) following the fall of Suharto's New Order regime (1998). The amendments established presidential elections by direct vote (previously through MPR), created the Constitutional Court (Mahkamah Konstitusi), strengthened human rights protections (Chapter XA), and set civilian control over the military. Indonesia is now a presidential republic: President directly elected, maximum two 5-year terms. The Constitutional Court has been active in striking down laws — notably overturning adultery and cohabitation criminalization attempts. Indonesia is the world's largest Muslim-majority democracy.
laws.penalty: Constitutional rights violations by state actors: judicial review available at Constitutional Court. Challenging the unitary state (NKRI): treason charges under Criminal Code.
exceptions: Regional autonomy provisions allow significant decentralization to provinces and regencies
Special regions (Aceh, Papua, Yogyakarta) have distinct constitutional status
Transitional justice for historical human rights violations handled through separate mechanisms
laws.sourceLabel: Mahkamah Konstitusi — Constitutional Court of Indonesia

quiz.q: What constitutional reform came from Indonesia's 1998 democratic transition?
options: Indonesia shifted from presidential to parliamentary system
Presidential elections changed to direct popular vote, Constitutional Court created, and human rights chapter added
Indonesia became a federal state giving regions full autonomy
The military was given reserved seats in parliament
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's 1999-2002 constitutional amendments were transformative: the president became directly elected by citizens (instead of by the 700-member MPR assembly), a Constitutional Court was created to adjudicate constitutional questions and electoral disputes, a human rights chapter was added, and civilian control over the military was strengthened. These changes turned Suharto's 'guided democracy' into a genuine direct democracy.

laws.title: KUHP Baru — New Indonesian Penal Code (2023)
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's major criminal law reform including controversial moral provisions
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's New Penal Code (passed 2022, effective 2025) replaces the colonial Dutch-era Wetboek van Strafrecht (1918). The new code introduced controversial provisions: criminalization of extramarital sex (cohabitation outside marriage and sex between unmarried couples), insulting the President, and 'disturbing public order'. LGBTQ+ rights are not recognized; same-sex relations could potentially be prosecuted under morality provisions. Sharia-influenced provisions reflect Indonesia's Muslim majority. The code triggered concerns from tourism industry, human rights groups, and foreign governments — Indonesia's major tourism revenue (pre-COVID: $20B+/year) could be affected. Implementation is staggered: some provisions take effect later.
laws.penalty: Extramarital sex: up to 1 year imprisonment. Cohabitation outside marriage: up to 6 months. Insulting the President: up to 3 years. Blasphemy: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Only complaints from parents, spouses, or children can trigger prosecution for cohabitation/extramarital sex provisions
Tourists in international hotels in major tourist areas practically unlikely to face enforcement
Foreign nationals retain consular access rights
laws.sourceLabel: Kejaksaan Agung — Attorney General of Indonesia

quiz.q: What controversial new offense did Indonesia's 2023 Penal Code introduce that raised concerns for tourism?
options: Prohibition on foreign visitors photographing government buildings
Criminalization of extramarital sex and cohabitation outside marriage
Mandatory religious observance for all Indonesia residents
Prohibition on alcohol consumption by all persons regardless of religion
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's new Penal Code criminalized cohabitation outside marriage and extramarital sex — provisions not in the old colonial-era code. While enforcement requires a complaint from a spouse, parent, or child (limiting random prosecution), foreign governments and Indonesia's tourism industry raised concerns about impact on Bali and other tourist destinations popular with foreign visitors. The code reflects conservative Islamic values increasingly influencing Indonesian law.

laws.title: Omnibus Law — Job Creation Law
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's sweeping economic reform reducing regulatory barriers
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Omnibus Law on Job Creation (2020, revised 2022) amended 79 laws in one statute — unprecedented in Indonesian legislative history. Key reforms: reduced severance pay requirements (maximum 19 months, down from 32), allowed fixed-term contracts for any type of work, simplified business licensing through an online single submission (OSS) system, relaxed foreign investment restrictions, and created Special Economic Zones with relaxed labor rules. The Constitutional Court initially declared the process procedurally flawed (November 2021); the government revised and re-enacted it in 2022. Labor unions and civil society strongly opposed, staging major strikes. Indonesia aims to shift from resource-export dependence to manufacturing.
laws.penalty: Operating without required OSS license: administrative fines and business closure. Environmental violations in investment activities: criminal prosecution under environmental law.
exceptions: Small and micro enterprises have simplified licensing through OSS risk-based approach
Investments in strategic national projects (PSN) have expedited approval processes
Foreign investment restrictions lifted for most sectors except those on negative list

quiz.q: What was unprecedented about Indonesia's 2020 Omnibus Law on Job Creation?
options: It was the first law passed by direct referendum in Indonesia
It amended 79 separate laws in one statute — unprecedented in Indonesian legislative history
It created a single national court for all labor disputes
It unified Indonesia's 34 provinces into 10 regional economies
quiz.explanation: The Omnibus Law amended 79 different laws simultaneously in a single statute — a legislative technique new to Indonesia, borrowed from common law systems. This allowed sweeping regulatory reform that would have taken years through individual law amendments. The Constitutional Court criticized the hasty drafting process (which excluded public participation required by law), but the substantive reforms were maintained in the revised 2022 version.

laws.title: Undang-Undang Kehutanan — Forestry Law
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's forests — world's third largest — under deforestation pressure
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia has the world's third-largest tropical rainforest (after Amazon and Congo Basin). Indonesia's Forestry Law (1999) and subsequent regulations govern forest management. Despite this, Indonesia experienced some of the world's highest deforestation rates in the 2000s-2010s: palm oil expansion, pulp and paper plantations, and illegal logging destroyed primary forest. Indonesia declared a moratorium on new primary forest and peatland concessions (2011, made permanent 2019). Peatland fires — particularly in 2015 when haze affected 6 countries and caused $16B in economic damage — led to the Peatland Restoration Agency. Indonesia committed to 29-41% emissions reduction by 2030.
laws.penalty: Illegal logging: up to 15 years imprisonment and Rp5B fine. Illegal clearing of state forest: up to 10 years. Palm oil company causing fires: criminal prosecution and license revocation.
exceptions: Customary forest rights (hutan adat) for indigenous communities recognized under Constitutional Court ruling
Community-based forest management permitted in production forests
Timber from certified sustainable forestry (SVLK) may be exported

quiz.q: What made Indonesia's 2015 peatland fires exceptional in regional impact?
options: They destroyed 10% of Indonesia's remaining primary forest in one year
Smoke haze affected 6 countries and caused an estimated $16 billion in economic damage
They triggered a tsunami through destabilized coastal peatlands
Indonesian fires caused measurable temperature rise across the entire ASEAN region
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's 2015 peatland fires were catastrophic: smoke haze blanketed 6 countries (Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Cambodia, Philippines), caused an estimated $16 billion in economic losses, killed hundreds, and exposed hundreds of millions to dangerous air quality. Burning drained peatlands released enormous amounts of stored carbon. The disaster finally prompted Indonesia to establish the Peatland Restoration Agency and take more serious action on peat drainage.

laws.title: Undang-Undang Informasi dan Transaksi Elektronik — ITE Law
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's controversial internet crime and defamation provisions
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Information and Electronic Transactions Law (ITE, 2008, amended 2016) criminalizes online defamation, offensive or immoral electronic content, and cybercrime. The defamation and 'morality' provisions (Articles 27-28) have been widely abused: used by powerful figures to silence critics, by husbands to prosecute wives, and by officials to silence journalists. Indonesia had 300+ ITE defamation cases by 2021. High-profile cases: a Buddhist woman sentenced for complaining about mosque loudspeakers on Facebook; a mother sentenced for defending her son against rape allegations. President Jokowi promised reform; 2022 amendments narrowed but did not eliminate the problematic provisions.
laws.penalty: Online defamation: up to 4 years imprisonment. Distributing 'immoral' content: up to 6 years. Hate speech online targeting ethnic/religious groups: up to 6 years.
exceptions: Journalistic activities conducted under Press Law have some protection from ITE prosecution
Academic research and education purposes may qualify for content exemptions
Criminal complaints require minimum substantiation before police may investigate

quiz.q: What troubling use pattern emerged with Indonesia's ITE Law defamation provisions?
options: Foreign governments used ITE to suppress pro-democracy content in Indonesia
Powerful figures and officials used it to silence critics — including a woman jailed for complaining about mosque loudspeakers on Facebook
It was used exclusively against foreign social media companies operating in Indonesia
The law was used primarily to combat Indonesian piracy of international software
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's ITE defamation provisions became a tool for silencing criticism: politicians filed cases against citizens who posted critical comments on social media; companies sued employees who complained publicly; a Buddhist woman was convicted for Facebook posts about mosque loudspeakers (seen as interfering with her sleep); and mothers were prosecuted for online posts defending their children. The law chilled online speech far beyond its intended cybercrime purpose.

laws.title: Undang-Undang Penodaan Agama — Blasphemy Law
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's blasphemy prohibition and religious minority restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Blasphemy Law (1965) prohibits 'misrepresentation' or 'deviancy' from the five recognized official religions: Islam, Protestantism, Catholicism, Hinduism, and Buddhism. (Confucianism was added in 2006). Ahmadiyya Muslims — who believe in a prophet after Muhammad — have been labeled 'heretical' and their congregations banned in many provinces. Blasphemy prosecutions have increased. Former Jakarta Governor Basuki Tjahaja Purnama (Ahok), a Chinese-Christian, was convicted of blasphemy in 2017 for stating during a campaign that opponents were 'lying' using a Quranic verse — amid major protests by hardline Islamic groups. Atheism is effectively criminalized — the law requires all Indonesians to profess a religion.
laws.penalty: Blasphemy: up to 5 years imprisonment. 'Defaming religion': up to 5 years. Practicing a non-recognized religion: administrative closure of religious activities and potential prosecution.
exceptions: Academic study of religions including their histories and disputes is nominally protected
Foreigners following non-recognized religions in private settings generally not prosecuted
Indigenous religious practices (kepercayaan) officially recognized since Constitutional Court ruling (2017) but in practice still face discrimination
laws.sourceLabel: Mahkamah Agung — Supreme Court of Indonesia

quiz.q: What group faces persecution under Indonesia's blasphemy law for beliefs about prophethood?
options: Ahmadiyya Muslims — labeled heretical for believing in a prophet after Muhammad
quiz.explanation: Ahmadiyya Muslims believe in Mirza Ghulam Ahmad as a prophet after Muhammad — which mainstream Islam considers heretical since Muhammad is 'the seal of the prophets'. Indonesian authorities have declared Ahmadiyya 'deviant' and banned their activities in many provinces. Ahmadiyya members have faced mob attacks on their mosques (sometimes with police standing by) and criminal prosecution for 'blasphemy' for practicing their faith.

laws.title: Undang-Undang Ketenagakerjaan — Manpower Law
laws.subtitle: Labor protections and Indonesia's large informal workforce
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Manpower Law (2003, modified by Omnibus Law 2022) sets employment standards for Indonesia's workforce of 140+ million. Minimum wages are set by province and regency — Jakarta's is among the highest (~Rp5M/month). Indonesia has a large informal economy: ~57% of workers are informal (street traders, domestic workers, agricultural laborers). BPJS Ketenagakerjaan (labor social security) provides workers' compensation, old-age savings, and death benefits — but coverage is primarily for formal workers. Religious holiday allowances (THR, Tunjangan Hari Raya) must be paid before Eid and Christmas — typically one month's salary for workers with 1+ year tenure.
laws.penalty: Non-payment of THR: administrative fines 5% of THR owed. Forcing workers beyond overtime limits: criminal investigation. Child labor in hazardous work: up to 4 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Domestic workers covered by Domestic Workers Protection Act (separate from Manpower Law)
Micro and small enterprises have modified compliance requirements
Agricultural workers in smallholder farming have reduced formal employment obligations
laws.sourceLabel: Kementerian Ketenagakerjaan — Ministry of Manpower Indonesia

quiz.q: What is Indonesia's THR (Tunjangan Hari Raya) and when must it be paid?
options: A quarterly performance bonus determined by each employer
A mandatory holiday allowance equivalent to one month's salary, paid before Eid and Christmas
A government grant to workers earning below minimum wage
A tax-free travel allowance for workers returning to their hometown
quiz.explanation: THR (Tunjangan Hari Raya — Religious Holiday Allowance) is a mandatory payment to all employees before major religious holidays — primarily Eid (Lebaran) and Christmas. Workers with 1+ year tenure receive one full month's salary; those with less tenure receive a pro-rated amount. The Eid THR is particularly significant as Indonesian workers traditionally return to their hometowns (mudik), requiring significant cash. Non-payment is a serious labor violation.

laws.title: Undang-Undang Perbankan — Banking Law
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's banking sector after the 1998 financial crisis
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Banking Law was fundamentally reshaped after the 1997-98 Asian Financial Crisis, when 16 banks were closed overnight and the rupiah lost 80% of its value. Bank Indonesia (BI) serves as central bank; the Financial Services Authority (OJK, Otoritas Jasa Keuangan) oversees banking, securities, and insurance since 2013. Indonesia's banking sector includes state-owned giants (Bank Mandiri, BRI, BNI, BTN) and major private banks. Islamic banking (perbankan syariah) is a significant segment: Bank Syariah Indonesia (BSI, created by merger in 2021) is among the world's largest Islamic banks. Digital banks have proliferated. Deposit guarantee covers Rp2B per customer.
laws.penalty: Operating unlicensed bank: up to 15 years imprisonment and Rp200B fine. Bank fraud: up to 15 years. Insider lending above limits: up to 8 years.
exceptions: Cooperatives and rural credit institutions (BPR) operate under lighter regulations
Microfinance institutions for micro and small enterprises have simplified licensing
Digital-only banks may operate under OJK digital bank framework with modified branch requirements
laws.sourceLabel: Otoritas Jasa Keuangan — Financial Services Authority

quiz.q: What new large Islamic bank was created in Indonesia in 2021?
options: Islamic Development Bank opened its first Southeast Asian headquarters
Bank Syariah Indonesia (BSI) was created by merging three state bank Islamic units — becoming one of the world's largest Islamic banks
A Saudi Arabian Islamic bank acquired Bank Mandiri creating a joint entity
Indonesia nationalized all Islamic banking into a government-run institution
quiz.explanation: Bank Syariah Indonesia (BSI) was created in 2021 by merging the Islamic banking subsidiaries of three state-owned banks (Mandiri, BNI, BRI). With assets of ~$25+ billion, BSI became one of the world's largest Islamic banks and a major symbol of Indonesia's Islamic finance ambitions. Indonesia has the world's largest Muslim population (~230 million) but Islamic banking still represents only ~7% of total banking assets — the merger was part of an effort to grow this sector.

laws.title: Undang-Undang Narkotika — Narcotics Law
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's strict anti-drug laws and high-profile executions
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Narcotics Law (2009) imposes severe penalties including death for drug offenses. Indonesia attracted international attention with the 2015 executions of the 'Bali Nine' (Australian drug traffickers) despite intense diplomatic pressure from Australia, including Australia recalling its ambassador. Indonesia has executed dozens for drug offenses since reinstating the death penalty for drugs. Death row for drug offenses has included nationals from many countries. Indonesia's anti-drug agency (BNN) has broad powers. The law provides for 'rehabilitation' for minor drug users as an alternative to incarceration, but in practice punitive approaches dominate. President Jokowi declared an 'extraordinary drug emergency' (2015).
laws.penalty: Trafficking over 5g methamphetamine or 1kg cannabis: death penalty or life imprisonment. Manufacturing drugs: death. Import/export of drugs: death. Possession for personal use: 4-6 years and rehabilitation.
exceptions: Addicts who voluntarily report themselves to authorities may receive rehabilitation rather than prosecution
Rehabilitation is the primary sentence for personal use amounts
Medical cannabis and opiate research exemptions for licensed institutions
laws.sourceLabel: Badan Narkotika Nasional — National Narcotics Agency

quiz.q: What international incident illustrated Indonesia's firm stance on drug trafficking?
options: Indonesia refused to extradite drug traffickers to any foreign country
The 2015 executions of the 'Bali Nine' Australian drug traffickers despite intense Australian diplomatic pressure, including Australia recalling its ambassador
Indonesia expelled the US Ambassador for criticizing its drug laws
Indonesia's Constitutional Court struck down the death penalty for drugs but was overruled by Parliament
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's execution of Andrew Chan and Myuran Sukumaran (leaders of the 'Bali Nine' — Australians convicted of heroin trafficking in Bali) in 2015 caused a major diplomatic incident. Australia recalled its ambassador from Jakarta in protest. Despite pleas from the Australian PM, public campaigns about their rehabilitation, and international appeals, Indonesia proceeded with the executions — demonstrating the government's resolve to maintain the death penalty regardless of diplomatic consequences.

laws.title: Undang-Undang Keimigrasian — Immigration Law
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's visa framework and border management for an archipelago nation
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Immigration Law governs entry and residence in the world's largest archipelago (17,000+ islands, 270M population). Indonesia offers visa-free entry to 90+ countries for 30 days. The Bali & Lombok Tourism Authority pushed for a 'second home visa' (5-year multiple-entry) for wealthy foreigners. Indonesia introduced a digital nomad visa (E33G, 180 days, tax-exempt) in 2023. Overstaying tourists in Bali has been a recurring problem — Bali immigration regularly deports foreigners who overstay or violate visa conditions (including working illegally or 'behaving offensively'). The 'Bali bad behavior' deportation program has become high-profile on social media.
laws.penalty: Illegal entry: up to 5 years imprisonment and Rp500M fine. Overstay: Rp1M/day up to Rp60M then deportation. Illegal employment: up to 5 years for employee, Rp5B for employer.
exceptions: ASEAN nationals receive visa-free entry for 30 days in most countries
Investors under KITAS/KITAP long-stay permits have residency rights
Diplomats accredited to Indonesia have immunity and special entry procedures
laws.sourceLabel: Direktorat Jenderal Imigrasi — Directorate General of Immigration

quiz.q: What innovative visa did Indonesia introduce in 2023 targeting remote workers?
options: A 'retirement visa' for those over 55 with pension income
A digital nomad visa (180 days, tax-exempt on foreign income) to attract remote workers
A 'tech talent visa' for employees of Indonesian tech companies
A 'surf visa' specifically for professional surfers sponsored by surf brands
quiz.explanation: Indonesia launched a 'Digital Nomad Visa' (E33G) in 2023 offering 180-day stays with the key incentive that foreign-source income earned during the stay is not subject to Indonesian income tax. This was specifically designed to attract remote workers — particularly to Bali — who spend money in Indonesia but earn abroad. Several countries (including Portugal, Costa Rica, and Barbados) had already introduced such visas; Indonesia's offering was notable for explicitly exempting foreign income from Indonesian tax.

laws.title: Undang-Undang Otonomi Daerah — Regional Autonomy Law
laws.subtitle: Decentralization in Indonesia after the fall of Suharto
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's regional autonomy laws (1999, revised 2004, 2014) transformed one of the world's most centralized states into one of the most decentralized. Before 1998, Suharto's New Order was highly centralized — Jakarta controlled everything. Post-reform: regencies (kabupaten) and cities (kota) have broad powers over education, health, infrastructure, and local regulation. Special regions: Aceh has Sharia law authority; Papua has special autonomy with additional fiscal resources; Yogyakarta is a special region under the Sultan. The decentralization created 'little kings' (raja kecil) — corrupt local officials. In 2022, Papua was split into 4 provinces — a significant restructuring of the easternmost territory.
laws.penalty: Local regulations (Perda) exceeding regional authority may be annulled by central government. Corrupt local officials prosecuted by KPK (Corruption Eradication Commission).
exceptions: Aceh province may apply Islamic law (Sharia) — the only Indonesian region with this authority
Papua provinces receive additional autonomy funds and affirmative policies for indigenous Papuans
Yogyakarta's Sultan serves as hereditary Governor — an exception to elected regional heads
laws.sourceLabel: Ditjen Otonomi Daerah — Ministry of Home Affairs

quiz.q: What unique religious legal authority does Indonesia's Aceh province have?
options: Aceh may collect its own national zakat (Islamic tax) bypassing central government
Aceh may apply Islamic Sharia law — the only Indonesian province with this authority
Aceh's Governor must be a Muslim cleric (ulema)
Aceh is exempt from national law entirely and operates under its own constitution
quiz.explanation: Aceh's special autonomy (Law 11/2006) grants it the authority to implement Sharia law — the only Indonesian province with this right. Aceh has an Islamic morality police (Wilayatul Hisbah) that enforces Islamic dress codes, praying schedules, and prohibits khalwat (close proximity between unmarried men and women). Sharia courts handle family law. This was part of the peace agreement ending Aceh's independence movement that claimed 15,000+ lives from 1976-2005.

laws.title: Undang-Undang Pengelolaan Wilayah Pesisir — Coastal Zone Management Law
laws.subtitle: Managing Indonesia's vast coastline and threatened coral reefs
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia has the world's second-longest coastline (54,716 km) and the world's largest coral reef area (51,000 sq km, part of the Coral Triangle). Indonesia's Coastal Zone Management Law (2007, amended 2014) regulates marine spatial planning, fishing rights, and coastal development. Indonesia's coral reefs face severe threats: bomb fishing (muro-ami), cyanide fishing, bleaching from climate change, and pollution. Jakarta's sea level rise and land subsidence crisis: parts of North Jakarta are sinking at 25cm/year — the city may be uninhabitable by 2050, prompting Indonesia's capital relocation to Nusantara in East Kalimantan (beginning 2024). Palm oil and mining runoff devastates coastal ecosystems.
laws.penalty: Bomb fishing: up to 5 years imprisonment and Rp1B fine. Cyanide fishing: up to 4 years. Illegal coastal reclamation: demolition order and fines.
exceptions: Traditional fishing communities with customary sea rights have modified permit requirements
Artisanal fishing vessels under 10 gross tonnes have simplified licensing
Emergency coastal protection works to prevent flooding may proceed without full planning permission
laws.sourceLabel: Kementerian Kelautan dan Perikanan — Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries

quiz.q: What crisis is causing Indonesia to relocate its capital from Jakarta to Nusantara?
options: Jakarta's population has exceeded 30 million making it ungovernable
Jakarta's sea level rise plus land subsidence (up to 25cm/year) risks making parts of the city uninhabitable by 2050
Jakarta's air pollution has reached dangerous levels requiring immediate city-wide shutdown
Jakarta's colonial-era street grid cannot handle modern traffic
quiz.explanation: Jakarta faces an existential threat: sea level rise from climate change combined with rapid land subsidence from excessive groundwater extraction is sinking the city — parts of North Jakarta are subsiding at 25cm per year, and significant portions are already below sea level. Studies project uninhabitability by 2050 if trends continue. Indonesia announced the capital relocation to Nusantara in East Kalimantan (Borneo) in 2019, with government operations beginning in 2024.

laws.title: Undang-Undang KPK — Corruption Eradication Commission
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's independent anti-corruption body and its battles
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's KPK (Komisi Pemberantasan Korupsi, 2002) was created as an independent prosecution body for corruption after decades of endemic corruption under Suharto (estimated to have stolen $15-35 billion). The KPK pioneered 'Operation Sunset' and dramatic handcuff-and-walk perp walks (OTT, 'caught red-handed') that became famous in Indonesian media. KPK's independence was significantly weakened by 2019 amendments: it was placed under government oversight, and KPK investigators were forced to become civil servants (losing investigator independence). Several hundred politicians and government officials have been convicted including governors, ministers, and a Chief Justice of the Constitutional Court.
laws.penalty: Corruption with state loss over Rp100M: up to 20 years or life imprisonment. Receiving bribes: up to 20 years. Asset recovery: all corruptly obtained assets confiscated.
exceptions: Voluntary self-disclosure and cooperation (kronologis) reduces sentences
Administrative violations distinguished from criminal corruption
Statute of limitations: 20 years for most corruption offenses
laws.sourceLabel: Komisi Pemberantasan Korupsi — Corruption Eradication Commission

quiz.q: What made Indonesia's KPK famous for its corruption arrests before its independence was weakened?
options: The KPK used advanced blockchain technology to trace corrupt money flows
OTT ('caught red-handed') operations — dramatic handcuff-and-walk arrests of officials caught accepting bribes, filmed for maximum publicity
The KPK had the world's highest conviction rate of any anti-corruption body
The KPK operated undercover agents in every government ministry
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's KPK became famous for OTT (Operasi Tangkap Tangan — 'caught red-handed' operations): staking out officials receiving bribes, catching them in the act, handcuffing them, and walking them out in front of TV cameras with the evidence bags prominently displayed. These dramatic scenes became a media staple and sent a deterrent message. The high-profile nature of arrests of governors, ministers, and judges demonstrated that no official was immune — a significant break from Suharto-era impunity.

laws.title: Undang-Undang Pokok Agraria — Basic Agrarian Law
laws.subtitle: Land rights in Indonesia's land-rich but conflict-prone system
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Basic Agrarian Law (UUPA, 1960) established the national land rights system. Land is categorized by title type: Hak Milik (freehold, only Indonesian citizens), Hak Guna Bangunan (building use rights, 30 years renewable for foreigners), Hak Guna Usaha (cultivation rights for plantations). Foreign individuals and companies cannot hold Hak Milik — only building use or cultivation rights. Land conflicts are pervasive: indigenous communities versus palm oil companies, farmers versus government projects. Indonesia's National Land Agency (BPN) manages registration. The 2020 Agrarian Reform Taskforce aimed to redistribute 4.5 million hectares to landless farmers.
laws.penalty: Land squatting: criminal prosecution. Environmental destruction during land conversion: up to 10 years imprisonment. Forging land certificates: up to 7 years.
exceptions: Customary (adat) land rights recognized in principle but registration complex in practice
Government may acquire land for public purposes with compensation under Land Acquisition Law
Foreign married to Indonesian citizen may indirectly access Hak Milik through spouse
laws.sourceLabel: Kementerian ATR/BPN — Ministry of Agrarian Affairs and Spatial Planning

quiz.q: What type of land title is restricted to Indonesian citizens only?
options: Hak Guna Bangunan (building rights) — foreigners cannot build
Hak Milik (freehold title) — only Indonesian citizens may hold full ownership
Hak Sewa (lease rights) — forbidden to foreigners
All land rights are open to foreign nationals on equal terms with Indonesians
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's Basic Agrarian Law reserves Hak Milik (freehold, permanent ownership) exclusively for Indonesian citizens. Foreigners may hold Hak Guna Bangunan (30-year building rights) or Hak Guna Usaha (cultivation rights for plantations). This limitation on foreign land ownership has practical workarounds — nominee arrangements, long leases, HGB over Hak Milik land — but legal ownership remains restricted, a deliberate post-colonial policy decision.

laws.title: Undang-Undang Kesehatan — Health Law
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's universal health program and healthcare challenges
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia launched Jaminan Kesehatan Nasional (JKN, National Health Insurance) in 2014, aiming for universal coverage. JKN is managed by BPJS Kesehatan and has grown to cover 250+ million people — among the world's largest single-payer health systems. JKN has faced financial deficits due to adverse selection (sick people more likely to enroll than healthy). Indonesia's Healthcare Law (2023) introduced major reforms including greater private sector participation, requirements for pharmaceutical companies to invest in domestic production, and telemedicine frameworks. Significant disparities exist between Java and outer islands: specialist availability, hospital beds, and health outcomes vary dramatically.
laws.penalty: Operating healthcare facility without license: up to 3 years imprisonment. Practicing medicine without license: up to 3 years and Rp100M fine. Medical records falsification: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Remote area practitioners may have emergency prescription authority beyond normal scope
Traditional medicine (jamu and traditional healing) has separate, lighter regulatory track
Telemedicine consultations have modified prescription and practice scope rules
laws.sourceLabel: Kementerian Kesehatan — Ministry of Health Indonesia

quiz.q: What financial problem did Indonesia's JKN universal health insurance face?
options: The government could not collect premiums from informal workers
Adverse selection — sick people enrolling while healthy people opt out — caused persistent financial deficits
Private hospitals refused to accept JKN patients
JKN's benefits were too generous for Indonesia's economic level
quiz.explanation: JKN faced classic insurance adverse selection: people with health conditions enrolled enthusiastically (high claims), while healthy people — particularly informal workers not compulsorily enrolled — delayed or avoided enrollment (low premiums collected). This created persistent deficits that required government bailouts. Solutions include mandatory enrollment for informal workers, adjusted contribution rates, and benefit package reviews. Indonesia's experience illustrates the fundamental challenge in achieving universal health coverage with voluntary elements.

laws.title: Peraturan Pemerintah No. 71 — Government Regulation on Electronic Systems
laws.subtitle: Data localization and platform accountability rules in Indonesia
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Government Regulation 71 on Electronic Systems and Transactions (PP 71/2019) and related regulations require electronic service providers (ESPs) to register with the Ministry of Communications (Kominfo), store 'strategic' data in Indonesia, and comply with content takedown requests within 4-24 hours. Kominfo made international headlines in 2022 by blocking Steam, PayPal, Epic Games, and other major platforms for failure to register — later reversed after public backlash. Indonesia blocked WhatsApp, Telegram, Twitter, and other platforms periodically for content violations. With 200+ million internet users, Indonesia is a major market where platforms must navigate government content demands.
laws.penalty: Failure to register as ESP: government blocking of service. Non-compliance with data localization for strategic data: service suspension. Non-takedown of prohibited content within deadline: service blocking.
exceptions: Research and educational sites have simplified registration requirements
Small-scale electronic service providers under revenue threshold have lighter requirements
Personal blogs and non-commercial websites exempt from commercial ESP registration

quiz.q: What major platforms did Indonesia's Kominfo block in 2022 for failing to register as Electronic Service Providers?
options: Google, Apple, and Microsoft were blocked for tax avoidance
Steam, PayPal, Epic Games and others were blocked for failure to register — reversed after massive public backlash
TikTok and Instagram were blocked for hosting political content
Pornhub and adult sites were blocked under morality provisions
quiz.explanation: In July 2022, Kominfo blocked Steam, PayPal, Epic Games, Origin, Yahoo, and other major international platforms for failing to register as Electronic Service Providers by the deadline. The block on PayPal and Steam caused immediate public outrage — millions of Indonesians couldn't make payments or access games. Kominfo reversed most blocks within days after intense public pressure, highlighting the tension between internet regulation and the practical needs of Indonesian digital consumers and businesses.

laws.title: Undang-Undang Pemilu — Election Law and Indonesia's Democratic Framework
laws.subtitle: Managing elections in the world's largest simultaneous vote
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia holds the world's largest simultaneous elections: in 2024, 205 million registered voters elected the President, Vice President, 580 DPR seats, 136 DPD seats, and 2,372 provincial and local legislative seats — all on the same day. The General Elections Commission (KPU) manages elections. Indonesia abolished electoral threshold debates: parties need 4% of DPR votes to form a faction. The 2024 election saw Defense Minister Prabowo Subianto win the presidency — significant given his history of alleged human rights violations during the Suharto era. Campaign finance is regulated but dark money flows through party structures.
laws.penalty: Electoral fraud: up to 6 years imprisonment. Voter bribery (money politics): up to 3 years imprisonment and Rp36M fine. Intimidating voters: up to 3 years.
exceptions: Non-partisan civil society monitoring organizations have special accreditation status
Official quick count (hitung cepat) permitted by accredited pollsters
Electronic voting piloted in some regions; fully paper-based nationally
laws.sourceLabel: Komisi Pemilihan Umum — General Elections Commission

quiz.q: What makes Indonesia's simultaneous elections historically unprecedented in scale?
options: Indonesia holds continuous rolling elections over a full year
205 million voters elected President, Senate, parliament, and thousands of local officials on the same day
Indonesia is the only country with mandatory voting for all citizens
Indonesia holds elections every 3 years — the world's most frequent democratic cycles
quiz.explanation: Indonesia's 2024 simultaneous elections — held February 14 — had 205 million registered voters simultaneously electing the President/VP, 580 national parliament members, 136 regional representatives, and 2,372 provincial/local legislative seats. With 820,000+ polling stations and millions of poll workers counting paper ballots by hand overnight, it was logistically the world's most complex single-day democratic exercise. Previous elections were already large; combining all levels simultaneously amplified the scale.

laws.title: Undang-Undang Minyak dan Gas Bumi — Oil and Gas Law
laws.subtitle: Indonesia's energy sector and Pertamina's dominance
laws.fullDescription: Indonesia's Oil and Gas Law (2001) governs hydrocarbon extraction. Pertamina — the state oil company — is required to participate in all upstream contracts. Indonesia has contracted production sharing agreements (PSA) with major IOCs (international oil companies). Indonesia was once a major OPEC member but became a net oil importer in 2004 as production declined and domestic consumption rose. The Constitutional Court struck down parts of the 2001 Oil and Gas Law in 2012, finding privatization provisions violated the constitution. Downstream petroleum (refining, distribution) was partially opened to private investment. Indonesia heavily subsidizes fuel (pertalite, solar) — costing Rp500T+ annually — creating fiscal pressure. Coal remains Indonesia's largest export.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized petroleum extraction: criminal prosecution and asset forfeiture. Illegal fuel distribution without license: up to 6 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Pertamina has first right to participate in all new production areas
Community natural gas utilization in remote areas has subsidized pricing
Biofuel mandates (30% biodiesel in automotive diesel) create modified petroleum blending rules
laws.sourceLabel: Kementerian Energi dan Sumber Daya Mineral

quiz.q: When did Indonesia shift from being an oil exporter to a net oil importer, and why?
options: Indonesia never exported oil — it was always an importer
In 2004, when domestic consumption growth exceeded declining production from aging fields
In 1999, after the Asian Financial Crisis destroyed investment in oil exploration
Indonesia still exports more oil than it imports — the country is an OPEC member
quiz.explanation: Indonesia left OPEC and became a net oil importer around 2004 — a dramatic reversal.
